claims.claim: oRGs highly express a specialized transcriptional factor, HOPX on top of the pan-RG markers PAX6 and SOX2.
claims.source: Since oRGs highly express a specialized transcriptional factor, HOPX (Pollen et al., 2015) on top of the pan-RG markers PAX6 and SOX2, it would be crucial to investigate the orchestrated crosstalk between HOPX-dependent transcriptional/epigenetic network and actomyosin-mediated cytokinesis in oRGs.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

results.result: Using MADM-based genetic labeling in E14.5 mouse neocortex, the authors show that Pafah1b1 heterozygous NPCs (Pafah1b1ko/+) display abnormal Anillin distribution during late mitosis, with loss of the normal Anillin-rich ring at the midbody. WT NPCs show normal 'U'-shaped Anillin enrichment at the midbody during basal-to-apical ingression, while Pafah1b1ko/+ NPCs lack this pattern. Pafah1b1ko/ko NPCs are rare and arrested at prometaphase/metaphase with dispersed Anillin.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 provide converging immunohistochemical evidence from MADM-labeled neocortical NPCs showing Anillin mislocalization in Pafah1b1 mutants. The use of MADM allows cell-autonomous assessment of different LIS1 dosages within the same tissue section, providing strong internal controls. The observations are consistent with prior literature (Kosodo et al., 2008) and supported by Figure 1A-C.

results.result: In WT-MADM neocortex, RhoA localizes to the apical cell membrane at metaphase and enriches at the midbody at telophase. In Pafah1b1-MADM neocortex, Pafah1b1ko/+ NPCs show unequal RhoA distribution skewed to one daughter cell, while Pafah1b1ko/ko NPCs are rare and show apical membrane-associated RhoA at prometaphase/metaphase. This indicates LIS1 contributes to cleavage plane specification during late NPC mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42 demonstrate RhoA mislocalization in Pafah1b1 mutant NPCs using TCA fixation to preserve active RhoA. The MADM system provides genetically defined cell populations, and the observations are supported by Figure 1D-E. The unequal RhoA distribution in heterozygous mutants is a clear phenotype indicating disrupted cytokinesis.

results.result: In control neocortex (Pafah1b1hc/+), NPCs undergoing vertical divisions show normal basal-to-apical Anillin ingression. In Pafah1b1 heterozygous mutant neocortex (GFAP-Cre; Pafah1b1hc/+), there is a reduction in vertical divisions (42% vs 84% in controls), and NPCs undergoing oblique/horizontal divisions show diffuse Anillin at both apical and basal membranes, with only one daughter cell retaining concentrated Anillin at the ventricular surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C48 provide quantitative and qualitative evidence of Anillin mislocalization in Pafah1b1 heterozygous mutants using NPC-specific conditional deletion. The reduction in vertical divisions is consistent with prior work (Yingling et al., 2008), and the diffuse Anillin pattern is clearly documented in Figure 2. The observations support a role for LIS1 in cleavage furrow positioning.

results.result: Pafah1b1-deficient NPCs (Pafah1b1hc/ko) show increased unequal inheritance of aPKCζ (68.8% vs 30.7% in controls), indicating an imbalance in symmetric versus asymmetric divisions. NPCs with horizontal cleavage planes also show less polarized aPKCζ along the apical-basal axis, suggesting mild alterations in apical polarity. This abnormal cleavage furrow positioning may lead to unequal distribution of cell fate determinants and increased asymmetric (neurogenic) divisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 demonstrate altered cell fate determinant inheritance using aPKCζ as a marker. The quantitative data (Figure 3C) shows a statistically significant increase in unequal aPKCζ distribution. The use of N-Cadherin holes to identify cleavage furrows is appropriate. However, the inference that this leads to increased neurogenic divisions is reasonable but would benefit from direct lineage tracing or neuronal marker analysis.

results.result: Live-cell imaging of Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs shows decreased successful daughter cell separation (18.7±8% vs 85.4±6.1% in WT) and increased binucleation (40.1±1.2% vs 5.1±3.1% in WT). Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs also show increased cleaved caspase-3-positive cells and 3-6 fold increased cell death by live-cell imaging, indicating that Pafah1b1 deficiency induces cytokinesis failure and apoptosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 provide strong quantitative evidence from live-cell imaging and immunocytochemistry (Figure 4A-C) showing cytokinesis defects in Pafah1b1 mutant MEFs. The large effect sizes and error bars suggest adequate statistical power. The use of both constitutive mutants and the observation of increased apoptosis as a consequence of cytokinesis failure is well-documented.

results.result: Acute deletion of Pafah1b1 using tamoxifen-inducible Cre (CAGG-CreERT2; Pafah1b1hc/hc +TM12h) shows decreased daughter cell separation (36.6±5.3% vs 69.4±4.3% in controls). A trend toward increased binucleation (25.8±6.4% vs 15.7±6.1%) was observed but was not statistically significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 demonstrate that acute loss of Pafah1b1 recapitulates the cytokinesis defects seen in constitutive mutants, ruling out developmental compensation. The daughter cell separation defect is statistically significant (Figure 4D), while the binucleation trend (Figure 4E) is not. The 12-hour tamoxifen treatment may not allow complete protein depletion, potentially explaining the milder phenotype compared to constitutive mutants.

results.result: Acute Pafah1b1 deletion in MEFs results in drastic cell shape oscillation during cytokinesis, similar to Anillin-depleted cells. The midbody initially positions correctly but then destabilizes and oscillates between daughter cells, with chromosome sets moving back and forth and prominent mitotic spindle rocking. This 'hyper-contractility' phenotype is caused by actomyosin hyperactivity. In one example, one daughter cell inherited two chromosome sets (binucleation) while the other underwent cell death.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C68 describe dramatic cytokinesis defects observed by live-cell imaging (Figure 5A-B, Videos 1-2). The comparison to Anillin-depleted cells is appropriate and supported by citations. The observation of chromosome oscillation and the specific example of asymmetric chromosome inheritance with one cell dying is well-documented. The term 'hyper-contractility' is properly attributed to prior work (Werner and Glotzer, 2008).

results.result: Quantification shows that WT MEFs rarely display oscillated cell membrane movements (3.6±3.6%), while more than half of Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs exhibit hyper-contractility phenotypes (56.2±8.4%). Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs frequently show cell membrane blebbing with larger blebs than WT. Acute Pafah1b1 deletion (CAGG-CreERT2; Pafah1b1hc/hc +TM12h) also shows increased hyper-contractility with membrane blebbing (40.5±8.4% vs 13.5±2.4% in controls).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C73 provide quantitative evidence of hyper-contractility and membrane blebbing phenotypes (Figure 5C-E). The large differences between mutant and control groups with relatively small error bars indicate robust phenotypes. Both constitutive and acute deletion models show similar defects, strengthening the conclusions. The merged DIC and fluorescence imaging approach is appropriate for visualizing membrane dynamics.

results.result: In WT MEFs, active RhoA symmetrically accumulates at the equatorial cortex and colocalizes with Anillin at the midbody during late telophase/cytokinesis. In contrast, 60% of Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs show cleavage furrow mislocalization with large polar blebs at ectopic sites. Aberrant cleavage furrows form asymmetrically at one side of the equatorial cortex, and binucleated cells display protruding polar blebs. RhoA decorates the membrane of all polar blebs, suggesting RhoA and actomyosin are primary signals producing aberrant membrane bulges.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C80 demonstrate RhoA and Anillin mislocalization in Pafah1b1 mutant MEFs using TCA fixation (Figure 6A-B). The observation that RhoA localizes to ectopic polar blebs is striking and well-documented. The inference that RhoA/actomyosin drive aberrant membrane bulges is reasonable given RhoA's known role in actomyosin regulation, though direct manipulation experiments would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: In WT MEFs, cortical P150glued (dynactin) is incorporated at the polar cortex but excluded from the cleavage furrow where Anillin localizes. In Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs, this reciprocal exclusion of polar P150glued versus equatorial Anillin is less obvious. Quantification shows reduced cells with cleavage furrow-associated Anillin in Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs (27.1% vs 72.3% in WT).
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 show altered dynactin and Anillin distribution in Pafah1b1 mutants (Figure 6C-E). The reciprocal exclusion pattern in WT is consistent with prior work (Moon et al., 2014). The quantitative data shows a clear reduction in normal Anillin localization. This supports the hypothesis that LIS1-dynein-dynactin complexes regulate cleavage furrow positioning, though the mechanism remains indirect.

results.result: During mitotic division of WT MEFs, LIS1 localizes to centrosomes in metaphase-to-anaphase and central MTs during cytokinesis with mostly cytosolic distribution, while Anillin accumulates in the cytokinetic abscission ring at the equatorial cortex. There is no substantial overlap of LIS1 and Anillin in intercellular compartments during late mitosis and cytokinesis, suggesting LIS1 may only indirectly regulate Anillin through F-actin cytoskeleton regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 address the spatial relationship between LIS1 and Anillin (Figure 7A-B). The lack of colocalization is clearly documented, though the authors note they could not perform direct dual immunostaining due to antibody limitations. The inference that LIS1 regulates Anillin indirectly through F-actin is reasonable given the lack of colocalization and known LIS1 functions, but remains speculative without additional mechanistic evidence.

results.result: WT MEFs show an F-actin zone at the midbody that colocalizes with dynein intermediate chain (DIC). In contrast, Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs have wider F-actin cortical patches at the midzone that extend to the polar cortex in one daughter cell, and central MT-associated F-actin fibers are evident.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 demonstrate F-actin mislocalization in Pafah1b1 mutant MEFs using phalloidin staining (Figure 8A, though labeled as Figure 7A in the text). The observations of wider, asymmetric F-actin patches and central MT-associated F-actin fibers are clearly visible in the images. This supports the hypothesis that LIS1 regulates F-actin organization during cytokinesis.

results.result: In WT MEFs, non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (NMHCIIA) at the spindle midzone overlaps with the F-actin focus zone. In Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs, MHCIIA distribution is diffused and dispersed at the spindle midzone. Quantification shows Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs have fewer cells with normal cleavage furrow-associated actomyosin patterns (29.7% vs 73.4% in WT) and more cells with ectopic actomyosin distribution (70.3% vs 26.6% in WT), indicating impaired cortical constriction and cleavage furrow mispositioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C96 provide strong evidence of actomyosin dysfunction in Pafah1b1 mutants (Figure 8B-C). The quantitative data shows a clear shift from normal to ectopic actomyosin distribution. The use of both NMHCIIA immunostaining and F-actin (phalloidin) staining provides complementary evidence. The inference that this leads to impaired cortical constriction is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Live-cell imaging of MRLC1-GFP (myosin regulatory light chain) shows that control MEFs accumulate MRLC1 at the equatorial cortex and contractile ring with normal constriction. Pafah1b1 CKO mutant MEFs (CAGG-CreERT2; Pafah1b1hc/hc +TM24h) show impaired Myosin II movements, with cleavage furrow ingression that regresses abnormally and fails to restrict at the equatorial cortex, resulting in chromosome missegregation. Multiple ectopic membrane bulges near the polar cortex suggest aberrant cytoplasmic pushing forces from ectopically located Myosin II.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C102 provide dynamic evidence of Myosin II dysfunction using live-cell imaging (Figure 9A-B, Videos 3-4). The observation that cleavage furrow ingression initiates but then regresses is striking and well-documented. The inference that ectopic Myosin II generates aberrant pushing forces is reasonable given the localization data, though direct force measurements would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: In severely affected Pafah1b1 mutant MEFs, there is uncoupling between chromosome segregation and cytokinesis. While normal cytokinesis proceeds with chromosome separation followed by equatorial constriction, in Pafah1b1 mutants, actomyosin-mediated hyper-contractility triggers cytokinesis progression even when chromosomes have not segregated precisely, producing binucleated cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C105 describe a severe cytokinesis defect where the normal temporal coordination between chromosome segregation and cytokinesis is disrupted (Figure 9C, Video 5). This observation is well-documented and represents a striking phenotype. The inference that actomyosin hyper-contractility drives premature cytokinesis is consistent with the other data showing actomyosin dysregulation.

results.result: Live-cell imaging of SEPT6-GFP shows that in control MEFs, SEPT6 enriches at the equatorial cortex and stays at the cleavage furrow ingression site. After acute Pafah1b1 deletion (CAGG-CreERT2; Pafah1b1hc/hc +TM24h), SEPT6 initially localizes to the equatorial cortex but then regresses, with weak accumulation accompanied by cortical deformation and chromosome oscillation. The frequency of cytokinetic failure with SEPT6 mislocalization increases 4.7-fold in Pafah1b1 mutants (66.7% vs 14.3% in WT). Intercellular cytokinetic bridges and binucleation from incomplete cytokinesis are observed only in Pafah1b1-deficient MEFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C110 demonstrate contractile ring component mislocalization using SEPT6 as a marker (Figure 10A-C, Videos 6-7). The quantitative data shows a substantial increase in cytokinetic failure with SEPT6 mislocalization. The observation that SEPT6 initially localizes correctly but then regresses is important and suggests that LIS1 is required for maintaining, not just establishing, the contractile ring. The conclusion that contractile ring components are not retained at the equatorial cortex is well-supported.

results.result: WT MEFs expressing constitutively active RhoA (CA-RhoA-GFP) display increased cytokinesis failure with Anillin mislocalization, similar to Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs. WT MEFs with GFP control show normal cytokinesis. Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs expressing dominant negative RhoA (DN-RhoA-GFP) show decreased cytokinesis defects compared to GFP controls. This implies Pafah1b1hc/ko MEFs display RhoA hyper-activation, and RhoA inhibition rescues cytokinesis defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C114 provide critical gain-of-function and rescue experiments (Figure 11A-B). The observation that CA-RhoA phenocopies Pafah1b1 mutants and DN-RhoA partially rescues the mutant phenotype strongly supports the hypothesis that LIS1 regulates cytokinesis through RhoA. However, the rescue is partial, suggesting additional mechanisms may be involved. The use of appropriate controls (GFP alone) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: The authors conclude that LIS1 plays a crucial role in regulating cleavage plane positioning at late stages of mitosis and cytokinesis by restricting the cleavage furrow at the equatorial cortex through inhibiting cell membrane hyper-contractility. LIS1 regulates RhoA and Anillin-ring localization during cytokinesis and acts as an upstream mediator of RhoA-actomyosin-contractile ring component signaling cascades. Loss of LIS1 results in RhoA hyper-activation and mislocalization of F-actin and Myosin II, generating hyper-contractility forces ectopically at the polar cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C116, C117, C122, C131, C135, and C138 represent the major conclusions of the study. These are well-supported by the extensive data showing: (1) mislocalization of RhoA, Anillin, and actomyosin components in Pafah1b1 mutants; (2) hyper-contractility phenotypes; (3) CA-RhoA phenocopy and DN-RhoA rescue experiments. The model that LIS1 restricts cleavage furrow positioning by modulating RhoA-actomyosin signaling is strongly supported by converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that LIS1 determines cleavage plane positioning through a RhoA-actomyosin signaling pathway, defining a novel molecular mechanism underlying spatiotemporal regulation of cell membrane contractility during mitotic cell division. The LIS1-RhoA-actomyosin pathway sets the apical NPC cleavage plane by enrichment of cytokinetic furrow proteins to the ventricular surface. Pafah1b1 mutant NPCs show mislocalization of RhoA and Anillin skewed to one daughter cell, potentially impacting cell fate determinant segregation and inducing an imbalance of symmetric versus asymmetric divisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C27, C147, and C148 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The evidence from both NPCs and MEFs converges to support this model. The connection between cleavage plane positioning and cell fate determinant segregation is supported by the aPKCζ data, though direct lineage tracing would strengthen this conclusion. The model represents a significant advance in understanding LIS1 function beyond its known roles in MT/dynein regulation.

results.result: The introduction establishes that heterozygous loss of PAFAH1B1/LIS1 disrupts neurogenesis and neuronal migration via dysregulation of MT stability and dynein function. LIS1 is a regulatory protein controlling cytoplasmic dynein and MTs with dual roles coordinating MTs and actin cytoskeleton. Pafah1b1 mouse mutants show defects in NPC division, mitotic spindle orientation, and cell fate. Prior studies suggest LIS1 functions beyond MT/dynein-mediated mitotic spindle regulation, affecting mitotic progression from M phase to anaphase/telophase and daughter cell separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C14 provide background context from prior literature. These are well-supported by appropriate citations and represent established knowledge in the field. The synthesis of prior work effectively motivates the current study's focus on late mitosis and cytokinesis, which had not been previously explored in detail for LIS1.

results.result: The introduction describes the established mechanisms of cytokinesis: MTs provide positional cues for cleavage furrow location, astral MTs and cortical F-actin transmit inhibitory signals at the polar cortex, RhoA functions as a master regulator recruiting contractile ring components (Anillin, Septin), and Myosin II generates constriction forces. When MT-F-actin coordination is perturbed, MT dysfunction induces actomyosin dysregulation leading to hyper-contractility and mitotic failure. The authors hypothesize that the LIS1-dynein-MT network may be essential for cytokinesis by fine-tuning actomyosin and cell membrane contractility.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C24 establish the conceptual framework for the study based on prior literature. The background on cytokinesis mechanisms is accurate and well-cited. The hypothesis (C24) is clearly stated and logically follows from the established knowledge about LIS1's involvement in both MT and F-actin regulation. This provides strong motivation for the experimental work.

results.result: The discussion notes that Pafah1b1hc/ko NPCs exhibit severe mitotic progression perturbation with cell cycle arrest and frequent apoptosis, necessitating the use of MADM mouse lines to study sparse labeled cells. Multiple in vitro studies have shown that genetic mutant MEFs are versatile and reliable cell types to investigate cytokinetic defects, including those in the developing brain, with examples of cytokinesis-associated phenotypes in MEFs with reduced protein doses of various genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 justify the experimental approaches used in the study. The rationale for using MADM is well-supported by citations to prior work showing severe phenotypes in Pafah1b1 mutants. The justification for using MEFs as a model system is supported by multiple citations showing that MEF phenotypes are relevant to brain development. This methodological justification is appropriate.

results.result: The discussion summarizes that Pafah1b1 mutant MEFs display abnormal phenotypes at late mitosis and cytokinesis with increased binucleation and cell death from failed cell separation. Cell shape oscillations and chromosome rocking are similar to Anillin-depleted cells. Pafah1b1 deficiency induces cleavage furrow mispositioning and failure to recruit contractile ring components. Cell shape oscillation and cytokinesis defects were previously reported in nocodazole-treated cells, suggesting MT or MT-actomyosin interface misregulation induces hyper-contractility. Pafah1b1-dependent cell membrane contractility may be mediated indirectly by dysregulation of astral MTs. RhoA, Anillin, and actomyosin components were mislocalized in Pafah1b1 mutant MEFs.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C130 synthesize the MEF findings and place them in context of prior literature. The comparison to Anillin-depleted cells and nocodazole-treated cells is appropriate and well-cited. The inference that LIS1 acts through MT-actomyosin interface regulation is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism remains somewhat speculative (C128). The summary accurately reflects the experimental findings.

results.result: The discussion notes that prior Pafah1b1 mutant mouse studies showed LIS1 modulates GTPase-mediated F-actin dynamics in interphase cells and post-mitotic neurons. Pafah1b1ko/+ post-mitotic neurons displayed F-actin dysregulation at leading processes and aberrant GTPase activities of RhoA-Rac1-Cdc42. Pafah1b1ko/+ MEFs exhibited abnormal RhoA GTPase hyper-activation. A recent Pafah1b1 knockdown fibroblast study showed F-actin dysfunction and focal adhesion disruption during migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 place the current findings in the context of prior work on LIS1's role in F-actin regulation. These are well-supported by appropriate citations and help establish that the current findings extend LIS1's known functions from interphase and migration to cytokinesis. This contextualizes the novelty of the current work.

results.result: The discussion reviews prior literature showing that RhoA GTPase regulates apical NPC niche integrity through F-actin at adherens junctions, and RhoA activity modulation alters mitotic spindle orientation in chick neural tube. In mouse apical NPCs, Anillin-ring constriction determines cleavage furrow ingression site, and Citron kinase and RhoA colocalize at the apical membrane where the cleavage furrow and midbody are positioned. Mutations in Citron kinase and Kinesin family members (Kif20a, Kif20b, Kif4) alter NPC cytokinesis and result in microcephaly. Dynamic movements of RhoA and cleavage furrow-associated proteins to the midbody is a key process regulating NPC cytokinesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C144 provide extensive context from prior literature on RhoA and cytokinesis in NPCs. These are well-supported by appropriate citations and establish the importance of the RhoA-actomyosin pathway in NPC cytokinesis and brain development. This contextualizes the significance of the current findings showing LIS1 regulates this pathway.

results.result: The discussion notes that in the developing neocortex, apical NPCs self-renew via symmetric divisions and produce post-mitotic neurons via asymmetric divisions. The orientation of the cleavage plane is thought to be a major regulator of symmetric versus asymmetric cleavage.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C146 provide established background on NPC division modes and the role of cleavage plane orientation. This is well-established knowledge in the field and provides context for interpreting the aPKCζ inheritance data. This background is appropriate and accurate.

results.result: The discussion notes that prior work showed Pafah1b1-deficient E14.5 neocortex had increased TUJ1-positive neurons and cleaved caspase-3-positive apoptotic cells, suggesting neocortical daughter cell fates and survival/death are sensitive to LIS1 expression levels. Pafah1b1-deficient E15.5 neocortex displayed cortical plate thinning with weak subplate formation. NPC-specific Pafah1b1 CKO mice had reduced upper-layer neurons, indicating Pafah1b1 deficiency leads to impairments in neuronal subtype specification and neurogenesis with cortical patterning defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C149-C153 cite prior work from the authors' group showing developmental consequences of Pafah1b1 deficiency. These are appropriately cited and help connect the cellular phenotypes observed in the current study to developmental outcomes. The inference that altered cell fate determinant segregation contributes to these developmental defects is reasonable but remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The discussion explains that Pafah1b1 deficiency at earlier time points (E9.5-E11.5) resulted in neural epithelial stem cell death via apoptosis due to disrupted symmetric mitotic division, so these earlier cells could not be studied. At mid-gestation (E14), vRGs had sufficient LIS1 to avoid severe mitotic catastrophe while still displaying robust cytokinetic defects with distorted cleavage plane and mitotic spindles.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C155 explain the experimental strategy and timing choices. This is a reasonable explanation for why the study focused on E14 NPCs. The observation that E14 vRGs have sufficient LIS1 to avoid complete mitotic arrest while still showing cytokinetic defects is important for interpreting the results and represents an appropriate experimental window.

results.result: The discussion connects the current findings to prior iPSC studies of Miller-Dieker syndrome showing prolonged mitosis in oRG but not vRG progenitors. The authors speculate that the specificity for oRGs may result from different LIS1 dose dependencies in mouse versus human, or from oRG-specific features like lack of apical endfeet attachment and rapid mitotic somal translocation suggesting dynamic cytoskeletal rearrangements. Gyrencephalic mammals have substantial oRG populations that exhibit unique mitotic features and promote neocortical expansion. oRGs highly express HOPX, suggesting future studies should investigate crosstalk between HOPX-dependent networks and actomyosin-mediated cytokinesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C162 attempt to connect the current findings to human iPSC studies and speculate about oRG-specific mechanisms. While the speculation is reasonable, it remains largely hypothetical (C157). The current study did not directly investigate oRGs due to their rarity in mouse, so these connections are tentative. The suggestion for future studies (C162) is appropriate but highlights that this remains an open question.

results.result: The abstract and introduction state that Pafah1b1-deficient neocortical NPCs and MEFs exhibited cleavage plane displacement with mislocalization of furrow-associated markers, associated with actomyosin dysfunction and cell membrane hyper-contractility. LIS1 acts as a key molecular link connecting MTs/dynein and actomyosin, ensuring cell membrane contractility is tightly controlled for proper daughter cell separation. Through imaging of Pafah1b1-deficient MEFs, severe defects in cleavage plane positioning and dysregulation of cell membrane contractility were found.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C25 represent summary statements of the main findings. These are well-supported by the extensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing mislocalization of multiple cytokinetic markers, actomyosin dysfunction, and hyper-contractility phenotypes in both NPCs and MEFs. The conclusion that LIS1 links MTs/dynein and actomyosin is supported by the data, though the molecular mechanism remains somewhat indirect.

results.result: The discussion concludes that this study provides key insights into underlying cellular mechanisms by which Pafah1b1 deficiency leads to impairments in neurogenesis as well as defects in neuronal migration.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is a summary statement of the study's significance. This is well-supported by the data showing that LIS1 regulates cytokinesis and cell fate determinant segregation in NPCs, which would be expected to impact neurogenesis. The connection to prior work showing neuronal migration defects helps place the current findings in a broader context of LIS1 function in brain development.
